name: Augustine of Hippo

seo.title: St Augustine of Hippo: his life, his real quotes and feast days
seo.description: Who Augustine of Hippo was, in plain words: the pears, the garden in Milan, his mother Monica, his real quotes and his feast days East and West.

band.lede: Teacher, convert and bishop of Hippo, who told his own restless story to God in the Confessions.

picture.alt: Augustine in gold bishop's robes looks up at a burst of light marked Veritas, a quill in one hand and a burning heart in the other, with books by Pelagius and Julian under his foot
picture.credit: Saint Augustine, Philippe de Champaigne, about 1645-1650. Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Public domain.
picture.creator: Philippe de Champaigne

card.line: Teacher, convert and bishop of Hippo, who told his own restless story to God in the Confessions.

filters.alias: hippo augustin aurelius augustinus doctor of grace confessions city of god

who: Augustine was a teacher of public speaking from North Africa. For years he chased pleasure, success and a religion that made sense to him. In a garden at Milan in 386 he finally turned to Christ. He became bishop of Hippo and wrote the Confessions, the story of his life told to God.

lines: Almost seventy, in under two years
Through St Stephen's relics at Hippo
He died in the third month

facts.label: Born
facts.text: **13 November 354**, at Thagaste in Numidia, today **Souk Ahras in Algeria**. He gives the day himself.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: At Thagaste. He went to school at Madauros, then Carthage. His mother Monica was a Christian. His father Patricius was a pagan until near the end of his life.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **28 August 430**, at Hippo, of a fever. It was the third month of the Vandals' siege of his city.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At Hippo, with Possidius there. The 1916 Roman Martyrology says his body was later taken to Sardinia, then to **Pavia in Italy**. The OCA says his relics lie today in San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro there.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Aurelius Augustinus**, his Latin name. **Blessed Augustine**, in the Russian Church and the OCA. **Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo**, in Greek. Often called **the Doctor of Grace**.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint and a Doctor of the Church to Catholics. On the Orthodox calendar as Blessed Augustine, and Saint in Greek calendars. Anglicans keep his day, and Lutherans remember him.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: Britannica lists **brewers, printers, converts and theologians**, and the Augustinian orders.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A bishop with a book and a pen. Often holding a heart, burning or pierced by an arrow. Sometimes with a child and a shell at the seashore, from a medieval legend.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: So much that scarcely any student could read it all, says Possidius. Near the end he reviewed **93 of his works, in 232 books**. His letters and sermons are not counted in that.

portrait.alt: A faded wall painting of a bald, bearded man in a white robe, seated on a curved chair and pointing to an open book on a stand
portrait.credit: Fresco of Augustine, about 550-600. Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.
portrait.caption: A fresco from about 550 to 600, painted over a century after he died. He points to an open book. Public domain.

typeNote: The test reads him as he was before his conversion, when he loved talk, jokes and reading with friends. In the test, the Spark's opposite is The Deep Well, and its example is his mother, St Monica.

west.text: In the **1916 Roman Martyrology**, on the last day of February: his body brought from Sardinia to Pavia.
In the **1916 Roman Martyrology**: his conversion, at Milan.
**Catholic** memorial. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: **Greek** churches and the **Church of Cyprus**, as Saint Augustine. The **OCA**, as Blessed Augustine. The **Russian Church** keeps it on the old calendar, which is 28 June on today's calendar.

feasts.note: The West keeps 28 August, the day he died. The Orthodox churches agree on 15 June, but no source we found says why. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later.

traits.title: quick to weep, and not ashamed of it
traits.text: He wept when the people of Hippo seized him to be ordained. He wept for his mother after she died. If anyone thinks that a sin, he wrote, “let him not laugh at me, but rather, if he be a man of a noble charity, let him weep for my sins against Thee”. On his deathbed he read psalms hung on his wall, and wept.

cite.text: Possidius, Life, chapters 4 and 31; Confessions, Book 9, chapter 12

traits.title: could not live without friends
traits.text: What held him to his friends, he wrote, was talk and jokes, kindness, good books read together, and even the chance “to differ at times without ill-humour”. After his baptism he always shared a home with others. First he lived with friends at Thagaste, then with his clergy at Hippo.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 4, chapter 8; Possidius, Life, chapters 3, 5 and 25

traits.title: no gossip at his table
traits.text: He had two lines written on his dining table: “Who injures the name of an absent friend / May not at this table as guest attend.” Once some bishops who were close friends forgot them and talked anyway. He told them sternly that either the verses came off the table, or he would leave in the middle of the meal. Possidius was at the table that day.

traits.title: the poor came first
traits.text: When the church's money ran out, he told the people plainly that he had nothing left to give the poor. He even had the church's sacred vessels broken up and melted down, “for the sake of captives and of the many who were in need”. Possidius says some people disapproved.

traits.title: changed his mind, and said so
traits.text: Near the end of his life he reread every book he had written. Whatever he now found out of line with the Church's teaching, “this he himself censured and corrected”, says Possidius. The result was two books of corrections, the Retractations.

traits.title: easily distracted, and honest about it
traits.text: He admits that a dog chasing a hare in a field could pull his mind away from serious thoughts. At home, “a lizard catching flies” could do it too. He went on to praise God for such tiny creatures, but he says that is not what caught him first.

said.lede: Two men knew him best. Possidius was his friend for almost forty years. Jerome, an older scholar, argued with him by letter for more than twenty years.

quotes.q: But I believe that they were able to derive greater good from him who heard and saw him as he spoke in person in the church, and especially those who knew well his manner of life among men.
quotes.who: Possidius, at the end of his Life. Reading him helps, he says, but hearing and seeing him helped more.

quotes.q: …you are challenging an old man, disturbing the peace of one who asks only to be allowed to be silent, and you seem to desire to display your learning.
quotes.who: Jerome, stung by the younger man's letters, about 404

quotes.q: Go on and prosper! You are renowned throughout the whole world; Catholics revere and look up to you as the restorer of the ancient faith, and—which is a token of yet more illustrious glory—all heretics abhor you.
quotes.who: Jerome, writing to him in 418, after years of sharp letters

quotes.q: I am struck with wonder at your wisdom, both in the books you have published and in this letter which you have not found it too great a burden to send me by way of intercession for those in distress.
quotes.who: Macedonius, a Roman official in Africa, granting Augustine's plea for a man in trouble

moments.title: The pears
moments.text: One night he and a gang of friends stripped a pear tree near his family's vineyard. The pears were not even good, and he had better at home. They ate a few and threw the rest to the pigs. Nearly thirty years later he spent pages of his Confessions asking why. His answer: the thrill was the theft itself. “To do this pleased us all the more because it was not permitted.”

moments.title: Nine years a Manichee
moments.text: In his nineteenth year he read Cicero's Hortensius and was “roused to a desire for wisdom”. As a student at Carthage he joined the Manichees, a sect he would later write against. He stayed with them nine years.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 3, chapter 4; Book 4, chapter 1; Book 8, chapter 7; Possidius, Life, chapter 1

moments.title: The friend who died
moments.text: Back home as a young teacher, he grew close to a friend he had known since childhood, and drew him into the Manichees. Within a year the friend fell ill with a fever, and he was baptised while unconscious. When he came round, Augustine joked about it. The friend told him to stop if he wanted to stay friends. A few days later he died. “Mine eyes sought him everywhere, but he was not granted them.” Augustine wrote, “I became a great puzzle to myself.”

moments.title: Lying to his mother
moments.text: He wanted to teach in Rome. His mother Monica followed him to the harbour, to stop him or to go with him. He told her he was only waiting to see a friend off. She spent the night praying in a chapel to St Cyprian by the shore, and he sailed without her. “And I lied to my mother—and such a mother!—and got away.”

moments.title: The bishop who read in silence
moments.text: Milan asked the prefect of Rome for a teacher of public speaking. The prefect, Symmachus, set him a test speech and sent him. In Milan he went to hear the bishop, Ambrose, for his style, and stayed for what he said. He noticed that Ambrose read without a sound: “his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were silent”. Later he saw God's hand in it all: “To him was I unknowingly led by Thee, that by him I might knowingly be led to Thee.”

moments.title: Take up and read
moments.text: As a young man he had prayed, “Grant me chastity and continency, but not yet.” Now, torn in two, he left his friend Alypius and threw himself down in tears under a fig tree in the garden. “How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now?” Then from a house nearby he heard a child's voice chanting, “Take up and read; take up and read.” He went back to where Alypius sat, opened Paul's letters, and read the first lines his eyes fell on, from Romans 13: “Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying; but put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.” He read no further. “All the gloom of doubt vanished away.” Alypius joined him that day, and they went in to tell Monica. “She leapeth for joy, and triumpheth, and blesseth Thee.”

moments.title: Baptised by Ambrose
moments.text: Ambrose baptised him at Easter. Alypius was baptised with him, a man so hard on his own body that he walked barefoot on the frozen ground of Italy. So was his son Adeodatus. The boy was barely fifteen, and his father says he “in wit excelled many grave and learned men”.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 9, chapter 6; Possidius, Life, chapter 1

moments.title: His mother's last words
moments.text: Waiting at Ostia for a ship home, he and Monica stood alone at a window over the garden and talked about the life of heaven. About five days later she fell ill with a fever. His brother wished she could die in her own country. She told her sons, “Lay this body anywhere, let not the care for it trouble you at all. This only I ask, that you will remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be.” She died there, in her fifty-sixth year. Augustine was in his thirty-third.

moments.title: Seized in church
moments.text: As a layman he kept away from any church that had no bishop, he later told his friends. Hippo had one, so he stood in the congregation without a care. But the old bishop, Valerius, told the people that the city needed a priest. They laid hands on Augustine and brought him forward, shouting, “while he wept freely”. Some thought he wept from wounded pride, because he was only made a priest. He said he wept at the dangers of ruling a church.

moments.title: Made bishop
moments.text: Valerius was old, and he was afraid another city would take his priest. Once he even hid him so that he could not be found. Then he wrote in secret to the primate at Carthage and had Augustine made bishop beside him. Augustine refused at first, because his own bishop was still alive. He gave way, and later said it should not have been done.

moments.title: The City of God
moments.text: In 410 the Goths sacked Rome, and pagans blamed the Christians. At the suggestion of his friend Marcellinus, he began his answer in 413. He worked on it for thirteen years. It grew into twenty-two books about two cities, one built on love of self and one on love of God.

cite.text: City of God, Book 1, preface; Book 14, chapter 28; Marcus Dods, translator's preface

miracles.lede: Two kinds of wonder are recorded. Possidius tells of healings through Augustine's own prayers. Augustine himself wrote down healings that he saw or checked, most of them at the shrines of martyrs, and he had the stories read out in church. He says why:

pledge.q: For when I saw, in our own times, frequent signs of the presence of divine powers similar to those which had been given of old, I desired that narratives might be written, judging that the multitude should not remain ignorant of these things.

items.title: Demons driven out
items.text: People asked him to pray for men possessed by demons. He prayed with many tears, and the demons left them.
items.quote: he entreated God in prayer with many tears and the demons departed from the men
items.witness: Possidius, his friend for almost forty years, says “I know also” that this happened.

items.title: The sick man
items.text: As he lay ill, a man brought a sick relative and asked him to lay his hand on him. Augustine answered that if he had any such power, “he would surely have applied it to himself first of all”. The man said a dream had sent him. So Augustine laid his hand on the sick man, and he went away healed.
items.quote: Go to the bishop Augustine that he may lay his hand upon him, and he shall be whole.
items.witness: The words the man heard in his dream. Possidius was in Hippo through the siege.

more.title: A blind man sees
more.text: At Milan, Ambrose was shown in a dream where the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius lay, and he found them. A well-known blind man of the city asked his guide to lead him there. He touched their bier with his handkerchief and put it to his eyes, and he saw again. Augustine was in the city at the time, and so was the emperor.
more.quote: The miracle which was wrought at Milan when I was there, and by which a blind man was restored to sight, could come to the knowledge of many

cite.text: City of God, Book 22, chapter 8; Confessions, Book 9, chapter 7

more.title: The surgeon's knife
more.text: Before he was a priest, Augustine and Alypius stayed at Carthage with Innocentius, a former lawyer. His surgeons had failed and said they must cut again, and he dreaded it. The night before, he threw himself down to pray with such sobs that Augustine could not pray at all, except for one line in his heart. Next morning the surgeon, knife in hand, searched for the place, and found it firmly healed. Augustine says it happened “in my presence, and under my own eyes”.
more.quote: O Lord, what prayers of Thy people dost Thou hear if Thou hearest not these?

more.title: The trembling brother and sister
more.text: Paulus and Palladia came from Caesarea in Cappadocia. Their widowed mother had cursed her ten children for a wrong they did her, and since then they shook in every limb. At Hippo they prayed daily at the relics of St Stephen. On Easter morning Paulus fell down as if asleep, and rose healed. On the third day after Easter their story was read out in church. Soon after, Palladia went to the shrine, fell the same way, and rose healed.
more.quote: The whole church was filled with the voices of those who were shouting and congratulating him.

doubt.title: Doubted from the start
doubt.text: People doubted then too. Augustine gives their question in their own words: “Why, they say, are those miracles, which you affirm were wrought formerly, wrought no longer?” Part of his answer is a jab. Whoever still demands wonders before he will believe “is himself a great prodigy, because he does not believe, though the whole world does”. He also admits that the new wonders stay local, “scarcely known even to the whole population in the midst of which they are wrought”.

words.note: Possidius says scarcely any student could read all he wrote. These lines are in the English of Schaff's Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, from the 1880s.

feature.kicker: The first page of the Confessions
feature.q: Thou hast formed us for Thyself, and our hearts are restless till they find rest in Thee.
feature.ctx: The Confessions are written as one long prayer to God. In Latin, {la|fecisti nos ad te et inquietum est cor nostrum donec requiescat in te}.

quotes.q: Too late did I love Thee, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love Thee! For behold, Thou wert within, and I without, and there did I seek Thee.
quotes.who: Looking back on the years he looked for God everywhere but within.

quotes.q: Two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
quotes.who: The key to his City of God.

quotes.q: Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?
quotes.who: He follows it with a captured pirate, who told Alexander the Great that he did with one small ship what Alexander did with a great fleet.

quotes.q: Once for all, then, a short precept is given thee: Love, and do what thou wilt.
quotes.who: Preaching on 1 John. He means that love must be the root of everything, even of correcting someone firmly.

cite.text: Homilies on the First Epistle of John, Homily 7, section 8

quotes.q: For understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe, but believe that thou mayest understand.

cite.text: Tractates on the Gospel of John, Tractate 29, section 6

quotes.q: O Lord the one God, God the Trinity, whatever I have said in these books that is of Thine, may they acknowledge who are Thine; if anything of my own, may it be pardoned both by Thee and by those who are Thine. Amen.
quotes.who: The last words of his On the Trinity.

myths.claim: “The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only one page.”
myths.truth: Not his. Quote Investigator traces it to Richard Lassels's travel book of 1670. Lassels only credited Augustine with calling the world a great book. Augustine did preach that creation is like a great book, meaning that it shows God. That line is under Where he stood, on nature.

myths.claim: “In essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity.”
myths.truth: Not his. The Augustine scholar James O'Donnell cannot find it in his works. It comes from the 1600s. Marco Antonio de Dominis printed it in 1617. Rupertus Meldenius used it about ten years later, in a plea for peace in the Church.
Not in his works. The nearest is his Exposition of Psalm 73 (72 in the Latin): one who sings praise does not only praise, but praises gladly, and loves the One he sings to.

myths.claim: “Pray as though everything depended on God; act as though everything depended on you.”
myths.truth: Not his. It is usually credited to Ignatius of Loyola, but it is not in his writings either. The earliest printing Trent Horn found is from 1868. A saying like it, turned the other way round, first appears in a collection of Ignatian sayings from 150 years after Ignatius died.

myths.claim: “Hope has two beautiful daughters, anger and courage.”
myths.truth: Not found in his works. Francis X. Maier says he could never find its source. A friend of his who is an Augustine scholar told him it is apocryphal.

myths.claim: He said we should love the sinner and hate the sin.
myths.truth: Not in those words. The nearest is a letter giving a rule to a community of nuns. Faults are to be corrected “with due love for the persons and hatred of the sin”.

myths.claim: He met a child on the beach trying to empty the sea into a hole, and learned he could never grasp the Trinity.
myths.truth: A late medieval legend. It is not in his writings, or in the Life by Possidius. William Caxton added it to his English Golden Legend in 1483. He had seen it painted on an altar at Antwerp, and he says he could not find it in the Latin.

myths.claim: He and Ambrose made up the Te Deum on the night of his baptism, singing verse by verse.
myths.truth: A later tradition, traced back only to the end of the 700s. The Catholic Encyclopedia says scholars now generally reject it.

rich.work: Sermon 61 (11 on the New Testament), section 10

calling.work: Sermon 100 (50 on the New Testament), section 2

pure.work: Sermon 73 (23 on the New Testament), section 4

rulers.work: Letter 185, The Correction of the Donatists, chapter 5

extras.title: The hard parts
extras.lede: Some of what he taught and did is hard to read today, and some Christians reject it. Here it is plainly, in his own words where we have them.

items.title: Forcing the Donatists back
items.text: At first he held that no one should be forced into the Church. By 408 he had changed his mind, and he backed the emperor's laws against the Donatists. What changed it, he says, was his own town. It had once been wholly Donatist. Fear of those laws brought it back, and now it would hardly believe it had ever been Donatist. He still begged judges to spare Donatists' lives, even men who had killed a priest. Of punishing wrongdoers in general, he admitted, “I confess that I make mistakes daily in regard to this.” In the 1680s these letters were used to justify the persecution of Protestants in France. The Archbishop of Paris had two of them printed. The French Protestant Pierre Bayle answered them point by point. He argued that Augustine's reasons for force were false. To change your mind because the laws worked was, he wrote, one of the worst ways of reasoning there is. He thought Augustine sincere and well-meaning, but carried away: “He had a great share of Knowledg, but he had more Zeal.”
items.quote: But this opinion of mine was overcome not by the words of those who controverted it, but by the conclusive instances to which they could point.

cite.text: Letter 93, to Vincentius; Letter 133, to Marcellinus; Letter 95, to Paulinus; Pierre Bayle, A Philosophical Commentary on Luke 14:23, the part on Augustine's letters (English translation, 1708), page 370

items.title: Babies who die unbaptised
items.text: He taught that anyone who dies with only the sin they were born with is lost, and that includes babies who die unbaptised. Their punishment, he held, is the lightest of all. Later Catholic theologians softened what the Church's International Theological Commission calls “the strict opinion of St. Augustine”. In 2007 the Commission found “serious theological and liturgical grounds for hope that unbaptised infants who die will be saved and enjoy the Beatific Vision.” It calls this hope, not sure knowledge. Pope Benedict XVI approved it for publication.
items.quote: the mildest punishment of all will fall upon those who have added no actual sin, to the original sin they brought with them

cite.text: Enchiridion, chapter 93; International Theological Commission, The Hope of Salvation for Infants Who Die Without Being Baptised (2007), sections 22 and 102

items.title: Hell that never ends
items.text: He held that the punishment of hell never ends, as the life of heaven never ends. Some Christians of his day hoped that all would be freed in the end. He argued with them, kindly but firmly.
items.quote: I must now, I see, enter the lists of amicable controversy with those tender-hearted Christians

items.title: Original sin and predestination
items.text: The OCA quotes two Orthodox scholars who sum up his teaching. Everyone inherits the guilt of Adam's sin. God is not bound to save anyone, and He chose whom He would save before they were born. Western theology built on this, the scholars add, from Aquinas to Luther and Calvin. Some Orthodox count it among his errors, as a question put to the OCA shows.
items.quote: Everyone is born guilty of the original sin.

cite.text: OCA, Questions and Answers, quoting Prokurat and Golitzin, Historical Dictionary of the Orthodox Church

items.title: The woman he sent away
items.text: For years he lived with a woman he never names, and they had a son. His mother worked hard to find him a wife. Then the woman was sent away, as an obstacle to the marriage. His marriage was still two years off, so he took another mistress while he waited. He tells it all against himself: he was “not so much a lover of marriage as a slave to lust”.
items.quote: And she went back to Africa, making a vow unto Thee never to know another man, leaving with me my natural son by her.

items.title: Sex and marriage
items.text: He counted marriage good, but a life without sex better. Britannica sums up the long debate: his views on sexuality “were humane in intent but have often been received as oppressive in effect”.
items.quote: marriage and continence are two goods, whereof the second is better

cite.text: Of the Good of Marriage, section 8; Britannica

items.title: No woman in his house
items.text: No woman lived or stayed in his house, not even his widowed sister, who led a community of nuns. Women who asked to see him met him only with clergy present. He said it was so that no weak person would be given a cause to fall, and no one could slander his clergy.
items.quote: No woman ever lived or stayed in Augustine's house, not even his own sister

circle.name: Monica
circle.text: His mother, honoured as St Monica. For years she wept and prayed for him. A bishop told her, “it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.” She lived to see him baptised, and died at Ostia soon after.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 3, chapter 12; Book 9, chapters 10 to 13

circle.name: Patricius
circle.text: His father, a pagan and a town councillor of Thagaste. Monica won him to faith near the end of his life.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 2, chapter 3; Book 9, chapter 9; Possidius, Life, chapter 1

circle.name: Adeodatus
circle.text: His son, born to the woman he lived with for years. He was baptised with his father at fifteen, and died young, within a year or two. Augustine wrote of him, “of me was there naught in that boy but the sin”. The rest, he says, was God's gift.

circle.name: Ambrose
circle.text: Bishop of Milan. “That man of God received me like a father,” Augustine wrote. Ambrose baptised him at Easter 387. Years later Augustine still kept rules he had learned from Ambrose: never find a wife for another man, and never urge anyone to join the army.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 5, chapter 13; Possidius, Life, chapters 1 and 27

circle.name: Alypius
circle.text: His closest friend, from Thagaste. He was beside him in the garden at Milan, read on from the same page, and turned to Christ that day too. They were baptised together. He became bishop of Thagaste.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 8, chapter 12; Roman Martyrology (1916), 15 August

circle.name: Possidius
circle.text: A monk of his house who became bishop of Calama. He tells of a bishop of Calama wounded in a Donatist ambush, without saying it was himself. He stayed in Hippo through the siege and wrote the first Life. They were friends for almost forty years, “with no bitter disagreement”.

circle.name: Jerome
circle.text: They wrote to each other for more than twenty years. Augustine questioned how Jerome read Galatians, and his new translation. The early letters were sharp. By 418 Jerome was praising him warmly.

circle.name: Pelagius
circle.text: A monk who came to Africa after the Goths took Rome. His followers were condemned at Carthage in 412 for attacking the teaching of original sin. He could not bear Augustine's prayer “Give what You command, and command what You will” when a bishop quoted it to him in Rome. Augustine wrote against his teaching for almost ten years.

cite.text: On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 53; Possidius, Life, chapter 18; Catholic Encyclopedia

circle.name: The Donatists
circle.text: A rival church in Africa, which baptised again anyone who came to it from the Catholics. Their armed bands, the Circumcellions, lay in wait for him on the roads more than once. One time his guide took the wrong road by mistake, and so he escaped.

circle.name: Origen
circle.text: Augustine rejected Origen's hope that even the devil and his angels would be freed in the end. He wrote that “Origen was even more indulgent” than the tender-hearted Christians of his own day, and that the Church, “not without reason, condemned him for this and other errors”.

circle.name: John Cassian
circle.text: Augustine's followers attacked Cassian's teaching on grace and effort. About 433, after Augustine's death, his defender Prosper of Aquitaine wrote a book against Cassian, whom the Catholic Encyclopedia calls “the soul and head of the whole movement”.

death.big: He died of a fever on 28 August 430, in the third month of the Vandal siege of Hippo. He was 75.
paras: The Vandals had crossed from Spain and laid Africa waste. Of all the churches of Africa, Possidius says, he saw only three still standing: Carthage, Hippo and Cirta. Possidius and other bishops took refuge with him in Hippo.
At table one day he told his friends what he was asking of God, and they all joined in his prayer. In the third month of the siege he fell ill with a fever.

He had the shortest penitential psalms copied and hung on the wall by his bed. He read them and wept. For his last ten days he asked to be left alone to pray, except when the doctors came or food was brought.

He preached until his last illness. His sight and hearing were sound to the end, and he died with his friends beside him, “while we stood by and watched and prayed”. He made no will, because he owned nothing. He asked again and again that the church's library be kept safe for the future.

later.title: After his death
later.text: After he died, the people left Hippo, and the enemy burned it. His books survived. Britannica says, “Somehow, essentially the whole of Augustine's literary oeuvre survived and escaped Africa intact.” The 1916 Roman Martyrology says his body was taken to Sardinia, and later to Pavia. Britannica is more careful about that: “Whatever the truth of the story”.

cite.text: Possidius, Life, chapter 28; Britannica; Roman Martyrology (1916), 28 August

items.q: I would have you know that in this time of our misfortune I ask this of God: either that He may be pleased to free this city which is surrounded by the foe, or if something else seems good in His sight, that He make His servants brave for enduring His will, or at least that He may take me from this world unto Himself.
items.ctx: Said at table to Possidius and the other bishops. Possidius adds, “In truth the Lord did not deprive His servant of the reward of his prayer.”

saint.big: Yes to Catholics and Anglicans, and Lutherans remember him. The Orthodox keep him on their calendar as Blessed Augustine, and Greek calendars call him Saint.

churches.note: A Doctor of the Church. Memorial on 28 August
On the calendar on 15 June. Saint in Greek calendars
A Lesser Festival in the Church of England, 28 August

paras: Catholics count him one of the four great Doctors of the Latin Church, with Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory the Great. In 1298 Pope Boniface VIII ordered the feasts of all four kept across the whole Church.

Some Orthodox say he was never a saint, because of his teaching on predestination. The OCA was asked about it. It answered that he is on the Orthodox calendar, and that a Moscow Patriarchate calendar lists him among the saints' names given at baptism. There, “Blessed” is a title, not a step before sainthood, as with Blessed Xenia of St Petersburg. The OCA adds that there is no record of a formal glorification, and that the Orthodox glorify saints in a different way. Its hymn for his day calls him “a lover of prayer, and a pillar of repentance”.

quotes.q: Blessed Augustine is respected in the Orthodox Church as a teacher, because of his wonderful defense of the Church's teachings against the various heresies of his time, but because of his errors in his teachings about predestination in the salvation of man, he was never considered a saint.

prayer.intro: From the prayer that opens his Soliloquies, written soon after his conversion, in 386 or 387.
prayer.q: God, from Whom to be turned away, is to fall: to Whom to be turned back, is to rise again: in Whom to abide, is to stand firm. God, from Whom to go forth, is to die: to Whom to return, is to revive: in Whom to have our dwelling, is to live. God, Whom no one loses, unless deceived: Whom no one seeks, unless stirred up: Whom no one finds, unless made pure.

kin.name: Philip Neri
kin.text: His biographer says he had “a very lively temperament, and without the least tendency to melancholy”. Philip hated idleness so much “that no one ever found him unemployed”. He welcomed all who came, rich and poor alike, and his room became known as “the Shelter of Christian Mirth”.
